data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A small team should adopt an existing experiment tracker only if their workflow is strictly observational; however, if the research involves active learning loops where the tracker must function as a real-time controller modifying experimental parameters, they must build a custom minimal tracker to avoid the 'integration tax' of forcing a causal control mechanism into a passive logging tool.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The team lacks the engineering bandwidth to maintain even a minimal custom state machine.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The active learning loop operates on a timescale slow enough to tolerate the latency of external API calls to a managed service.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The experimental parameters can be decoupled from the tracking logic via a robust middleware layer that already exists.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism relies on the distinction between 'passive observation' and 'active control.' Existing tools are architected as databases with UIs (passive), lacking the low-latency, bidirectional API hooks required for control theory applications. Attempting to wrap such tools introduces an 'integration tax'\u2014hidden engineering costs to hack plugins or manage state synchronization\u2014which creates a 'migration cliff' where early unstructured scripting prevents clean data schema adoption later. A custom build enforces a 'mechanist' causal model from day one, treating the tracker as the state machine itself rather than a log of states, thereby eliminating the single point of failure associated with mismatched abstractions.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
